paragraphs.heading: An antenna for the sky
paragraphs.text: A radio telescope is a special antenna and radio receiver that picks up radio waves from sources in space. It is the main instrument of radio astronomy, much as optical telescopes are for visible light. Unlike optical telescopes, it works in the daytime as well as at night.

paragraphs.heading: Why they are so big
paragraphs.text: Planets, stars, nebulas and galaxies are so far away that their radio waves arrive extremely weak. So radio telescopes need very large antennas to gather enough energy, plus extremely sensitive receivers. Most are big dish-shaped antennas like those used to track and talk to satellites and space probes. They can work alone or be linked electronically in an array. Observatories are placed far from big cities to avoid interference from radio, TV, radar, cars and other electronics.

paragraphs.heading: Jansky's merry-go-round
paragraphs.text: Bell Labs engineer Karl Guthe Jansky first detected radio waves from space in 1932, in Holmdel, New Jersey, while hunting for static that might disturb radiotelephone service. His antenna, an array of dipoles and reflectors about 30 m (100 ft) wide, sat on a turntable so it could point any way, which earned it the name "Jansky's merry-go-round". He sorted the static into nearby thunderstorms, distant thunderstorms, and a faint steady hiss. The hiss repeated every 23 hours and 56 minutes, one sidereal day, the time a fixed object on the sky takes to return to the same place. Comparing with star maps, he concluded it came from the Milky Way, strongest toward Sagittarius.

paragraphs.heading: The first dish
paragraphs.text: In 1937 radio amateur Grote Reber built the first purpose-built radio telescope, a 9-meter parabolic dish in his back yard in Wheaton, Illinois. The sky survey he made with it is often seen as the start of radio astronomy. After World War II, technology from the rapid growth of radar was put to work on the sky, and universities and research institutes began building large radio telescopes.

paragraphs.heading: Size depends on wavelength
paragraphs.text: How fine a detail a dish can see depends on its diameter compared with the wavelength it observes, and that sets how big it must be. Telescopes for wavelengths of 3 meters to 30 cm are usually well over 100 meters wide. Those for wavelengths shorter than 30 cm range from 3 to 90 meters across. For wavelengths of 30 down to 3 meters, the reflecting surface can be made of coarse wire mesh, even chicken wire.

paragraphs.heading: The giant called FAST
paragraphs.text: The largest full-dish radio telescope is China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST), finished in 2016. Its 500-meter dish lies in a natural hollow in Guizhou province and cannot move. Instead, a computer shifts 4,450 panels to reshape it, while a feed cabin hung on cables moves above it, so it can aim anywhere up to 40° from straight overhead. Only a 300-meter circle of the dish is lit by the feed antenna at once, so its effective aperture is 300 meters.
